meta.title: Install ai-jail and run your first jailed agent
meta.description: Install ai-jail with Homebrew, the AUR, cargo or Nix, preview the sandbox with a dry run, then start Claude Code or Codex signed in, with only its own API reachable.

hero.title: Install it, look inside, run your agent
hero.lede: ai-jail is one program with no daemon and no root. You install it, put its name in front of the command you already type, and the agent starts inside a sandbox.

install.title: Install
install.lede: Choose the way you already install command line tools. Every method gives you the same single ai-jail program.
notes: Works on macOS and on Linux.
The first package is a prebuilt binary for Linux x86_64. The second builds from source.
Needs a Rust toolchain. --locked builds with the dependency versions the release was tested with.
The first line runs an agent without installing anything. The second installs for your user. The flake points ai-jail at its own copy of bubblewrap.
The archives are signed, with checksums next to them. Unpack one and put ai-jail somewhere on your PATH. How to check the signature is on the Security page.

items.title: Linux
items.text: Install bubblewrap, the small program ai-jail uses to build the sandbox. Most distributions package it as bubblewrap.

items.title: macOS
items.text: Nothing to install. ai-jail uses sandbox-exec, which ships with macOS. Apple marks that interface as deprecated.

items.title: Windows
items.text: Not supported. Use WSL2 and follow the Linux steps inside it.

first.title: Your first run
first.lede: Three commands: a plan, a look inside, a working agent. The login is already inside, and ai-jail opens the route to the agent's API host for you.
first.alt: Three panels from left to right. Dry run: the cell is only a dashed outline and the agent waits outside. Look around: the cell is solid and holds a terminal and the project folder. Run the agent: the agent, the project and the agent's login card are inside, with one opening in the wall, a gate to the agent's API host that ai-jail opened itself. Your home folder stays barred outside in all three.
first.caption: Your home directory stays outside at every step, and the agent's login is inside from the start. In the last step ai-jail opens the one gate a cloud agent needs, its API host, when it knows the agent. The rest of the network stays shut.

steps.title: See the plan without running anything
steps.text: Go to your project and ask for a dry run. ai-jail prints the sandbox command it would use and exits. A dry run never writes a file.

steps.title: Look around inside
steps.text: Start a plain shell in the jail. Your project is there at its real path and you can edit it. Your home directory is a fresh one, and your shell's tokens are gone. Type exit to leave.

steps.title: Run the agent
steps.text: ai-jail mounts the agent's own state folder by default, so it is already signed in. When it knows the agent, it also lets one host through its filtered proxy, the agent's API: api.anthropic.com for Claude Code, api.openai.com for Codex, generativelanguage.googleapis.com for Gemini, api.x.ai for Grok, on Linux and on macOS. Telemetry hosts stay shut. On Linux, toolchains reach package registries such as crates.io, npm and PyPI by default, so builds work. --network opens the whole network instead.

steps.title: When you need more
steps.text: Put a host list in ~/.ai-jail, your own config file, under the agent's name. An explicit list replaces the default, so include the API host. Or use --network for the whole network. For a logged-out run, pass --no-agent-state. A .ai-jail file inside the project can only tighten the jail: it can shrink the host list and turn the login off, never the opposite, so a repository you clone cannot open the jail for itself.

gitignore.title: The .ai-jail file in your project
gitignore.text: An ordinary run may save project settings to .ai-jail. ai-jail never writes values you pass with --env to it. The agent sees that file as empty. The README suggests adding .ai-jail to .gitignore so git status stays clean inside the jail. Configure explains both config files.

exposure.title: What the defaults give away
exposure.text: The agent's login is mounted read-write, its API key variable (ANTHROPIC_API_KEY for Claude Code) is copied from your shell when set, and its API host is reachable, so anything running in the jail can use that login for the life of the run. --no-agent-state turns the login and the key off; --no-network closes the API host too. A host you allow is trusted for everything it offers: allowing github.com allows a push to any repository. --network is the whole network, so anything the agent can read, it can send. Your SSH keys, cloud credentials and other projects are still not there to be read. Security has the full list of limits.

see.title: What you will see inside
see.lede: The prompt changes to (jail) and the project is where it always was. Your toolchains are there too, read only. The things worth stealing are missing, except the agent's own login, which is there on purpose.
comments: # the project is at its real path
# a token exported in your shell did not come along
# your keys are not in this home
# the jail has its own hostname
see.note: This is a Linux session. macOS has no way to build a separate file tree, so there the same paths exist and reading them is refused.
see.alt: The view from inside the cell. The agent sits next to a large, bright project folder, with a fresh home and the system tools behind it. Outside the bars, dim and barred: SSH keys, cloud logins, other projects and the network.
see.caption: From inside, the project is the only thing of yours that you can change. Your toolchains (mise, cargo, npm and others) are there, read only, with a dependency cache the jail owns. The network stays outside, apart from a known agent's own API host and, on Linux, the package registries those toolchains fetch from, until you open a host with --allow-host or all of it with --network. How toolchains are mapped.

trouble.title: If it does not start
trouble.lede: These are the cases the README's troubleshooting covers, plus the two setup rules people trip on.

items.title: bwrap: setting up uid map: Permission denied
items.text: Ubuntu 24.04 and later and Debian 13 and later ship an AppArmor policy that stops programs from creating user namespaces without root, which is how bubblewrap isolates the jail. It affects every rootless tool of this kind. Relax it for the whole system:
items.alt: Or keep the policy and exempt only bwrap. Save this as /etc/apparmor.d/bwrap, then run sudo apparmor_parser -r /etc/apparmor.d/bwrap.

items.title: Your BWRAP_BIN is refused
items.text: You can point ai-jail at a specific bubblewrap with BWRAP_BIN. ai-jail accepts it only when it resolves to a program owned by root that other users cannot write, or to one in a standard multi-user /nix/store. It refuses a copy in your own home, because anyone who can replace that file controls the jail.

items.title: opencode hangs at Starting background server
items.text: opencode 2.x talks to a shared background server. The jail is a one-shot wrapper with a fresh home, so that server does not survive between runs. Start opencode self-contained with --standalone, and pin it in your config so you do not type it each time. ai-jail warns at launch when opencode starts without it:

items.title: Failed to create stream fd at startup
items.text: This comes from a login script on Ubuntu desktop during mise setup. It is harmless and mise still works. Pass --no-mise to skip mise setup and the message with it.

agents.title: Per agent
agents.lede: ai-jail knows where each agent keeps its login and mounts it by default: only the folders of the agent you start, and only if they exist. --no-agent-state turns it off. When set in your shell, that agent's API key variable comes along too: ANTHROPIC_API_KEY, OPENAI_API_KEY, GEMINI_API_KEY or GOOGLE_API_KEY, XAI_API_KEY, MOONSHOT_API_KEY.

notes.claude: For a second Claude profile, point --claude-dir at its directory.
notes.codex: After you resize the window, ai-jail sends Codex a redraw key so the screen repaints.
notes.opencode: Needs --standalone. See the troubleshooting item above.
notes.antigravity: Shares its Google login with Gemini, so one sign in serves both.
notes.kimi: ~/.kimi-code, the older location, is mounted too when it exists.
notes.aimemory: ai-jail recognizes the agent that ai-memory launches and applies that agent's settings, with both programs in one jail.
notes.kiro: On macOS the second folder is ~/Library/Application Support/kiro-cli instead.
notes.prime: Only the agent's own folder, never the whole ~/.prime.

agents.more: The same works for crush, grok, jcode, pi, aider, soulforge and omp. Any other command runs too, with the same jail and no login folder. ai-jail opens the API host by default for claude, codex, gemini and grok; other agents need --allow-host or --network.
